d: A severe drop in granulocytes (mainly neutrophils), the white blood cells that fight bacteria. Infections can become serious quickly.
An inner feeling of restlessness with an urge to keep moving, such as pacing or shifting the legs. A movement side effect of antipsychotics and some antiemetics.
Hair loss.
Absence of menstrual periods. Secondary amenorrhea means periods stop after they had been occurring.
A severe, whole-body allergic reaction that can cause airway swelling, trouble breathing and a drop in blood pressure. It needs emergency treatment with epinephrine.
Swelling in the deeper layers of the skin, often of the lips, tongue, face or throat. Swelling of the throat can block the airway.
Inability to form new memories of events that happen after a drug is taken or after an injury.
A pause in breathing.
Failure of the bone marrow to make enough red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Joint pain.
Fluid buildup in the abdomen, most often caused by liver cirrhosis.
Physical weakness or lack of energy.
Loss of coordination of muscle movements, causing an unsteady walk or clumsy movements.
Eczema: a long-lasting skin condition with dry, itchy, inflamed patches.
An irregular, often fast heart rhythm that starts in the upper chambers (atria). Blood can pool and clot in the atria, which raises the risk of stroke.
A hard mass of undigested material that collects in the stomach or intestine and can cause a blockage.
Reduced production of blood cells by the bone marrow, which lowers white blood cells, red blood cells and platelets. It raises the risk of infection, anemia and bleeding.
A heart rate that is slower than normal.
Breathing that is slower than normal.
Tightening of the muscles around the airways, which narrows them and causes wheezing and shortness of breath.
Disease of the heart muscle that makes it harder for the heart to pump blood.
Swelling of the brain caused by excess fluid.
Red eyes caused by widened blood vessels on the white of the eye.
A red, itchy skin rash where the skin touched a substance that irritates it or causes an allergic reaction.
Crystals forming in the urine. Some drugs can crystallize in the kidneys if the patient is not well hydrated.
Signs of too much cortisol, such as weight gain in the face and trunk, thin skin, easy bruising, high blood sugar and bone loss. Long-term corticosteroid use is a common cause.
Infection or inflammation of the bladder.
Black, sticky stools (melena). They usually mean bleeding in the upper digestive tract. Iron and bismuth can also turn stools black without bleeding.
A sudden state of confusion with reduced attention and awareness, which often comes and goes during the day.
Heavy sweating.
Double vision.
Flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache and a fast heart rate when alcohol is taken with certain drugs. The drug blocks the breakdown of acetaldehyde, a product of alcohol metabolism.
Lupus-like symptoms, such as joint pain, muscle pain, fever and rash, caused by a drug. Symptoms usually go away after the drug is stopped.
A changed or unpleasant sense of taste.
Involuntary, uncontrolled movements, such as twisting or jerking.
Abnormal levels of cholesterol or triglycerides in the blood.
Indigestion: discomfort or burning in the upper abdomen, often with fullness or bloating.
Hoarseness or difficulty speaking because of changes in the voice.
Shortness of breath.
Sustained, involuntary muscle contractions that cause twisting or abnormal postures, such as a neck turned to one side. A movement side effect of antipsychotics and some antiemetics.
Pain or burning when urinating.
Swelling caused by fluid trapped in the body's tissues. Peripheral edema is swelling of the legs, ankles or feet.
Rapid, exaggerated changes in mood, such as sudden crying or laughing.
A change in how the brain works, causing confusion, sleepiness or changes in behavior.
Infection of the inner lining of the heart, usually the heart valves.
Nosebleed.
Damage to the surface cells of the cornea, which can cause blurry vision or eye irritation.
Belching.
Redness of the skin.
Inflammation of the esophagus. Some pills can irritate the esophagus if they are taken without enough water or right before lying down.
Movement side effects of drugs that block dopamine: dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia.
Leakage of an IV drug out of the vein into the surrounding tissue. Some drugs damage or kill that tissue.
Passing gas.
Delayed emptying of the stomach without a blockage, causing nausea, vomiting and early fullness. Diabetes is a common cause.
Inflammation of the gums, with redness, swelling and bleeding.
Enlargement of breast tissue in males.
A collection of blood outside the blood vessels. An epidural or spinal hematoma presses on the spinal cord and can cause paralysis.
Blood in the urine.
Confusion and changes in behavior caused by liver failure. The liver cannot clear ammonia and other toxins from the blood.
Liver enzymes (ALT and AST) measured in the blood. Higher levels mean liver cells may be damaged or inflamed.
Damage to the liver caused by a drug or chemical.
An immune reaction to heparin that lowers the platelet count and, despite the low platelets, causes blood clots.
Too much ammonia in the blood, which can cause confusion and drowsiness.
Too much calcium in the blood.
High blood sugar.
Too much potassium in the blood. High potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
Too much sodium in the blood, usually from losing water.
Too much phosphate in the blood, common in chronic kidney disease.
Darkening of the skin. Periocular hyperpigmentation is darkening of the skin around the eyes.
Too much of the hormone prolactin in the blood. It can cause breast enlargement, milk discharge and missed periods.
An allergic or immune reaction to a drug, ranging from a rash to anaphylaxis.
A sudden, severe rise in blood pressure. It is called an emergency when it damages organs such as the brain, heart or kidneys.
High levels of triglycerides (a type of fat) in the blood.
Too much fluid in the blood vessels, which can cause swelling and fluid in the lungs.
Too little calcium in the blood.
Low blood sugar. Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, confusion and a fast heart rate.
The testes or ovaries make too little sex hormone. In males, low testosterone.
Too little potassium in the blood. Low potassium can cause muscle weakness and abnormal heart rhythms.
Too little magnesium in the blood.
Too little sodium in the blood, which can cause confusion, headache and seizures.
Lightening of the skin from loss of pigment.
Low blood pressure.
Less hair than normal. Eyelash hypotrichosis means thin or short eyelashes.
Too little fluid in the blood vessels, for example from dehydration or blood loss.
Inflammation of the tissue around the air sacs of the lungs, causing cough and shortness of breath.
The fluid pressure inside the eye. High intraocular pressure is the main risk factor for glaucoma.
During cataract surgery, the iris becomes floppy and the pupil shrinks, which makes the surgery harder. It is linked to alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin.
Given by injection into the fluid around the spinal cord.
Dry eye disease.
A buildup of lactic acid in the blood that makes the blood too acidic. It is rare but life-threatening.
A low white blood cell count, which raises the risk of infection.
Cancer of the lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell.
Anemia in which the red blood cells are larger than normal, often from a lack of folic acid or vitamin B12.
A rare inherited reaction to some anesthetics that causes a very high body temperature, muscle rigidity and muscle breakdown. Dantrolene treats it.
A type of thyroid cancer that starts in the C-cells of the thyroid.
Too much acid in the blood because of the body's metabolism, for example from losing bicarbonate.
Muscle pain.
An autoimmune disease that blocks signals from nerves to muscles, causing muscle weakness that gets worse with use.
Heart attack: heart muscle is damaged because its blood supply is blocked.
Inflammation of the heart muscle.
Muscle disease that causes muscle weakness or pain.
The common cold: inflammation of the nose and throat.
Death of body tissue.
Withdrawal symptoms in a newborn whose mother used opioids during pregnancy, such as irritability, tremor, poor feeding and diarrhea.
Damage to the kidneys caused by a drug or chemical.
Birth defects of the brain or spinal cord, such as spina bifida. Folic acid before and during early pregnancy lowers the risk.
Pain caused by damaged nerves, often described as burning, shooting or tingling.
Damage to the brain or nerves caused by a drug or chemical.
A low count of neutrophils, the white blood cells that fight bacterial infections.
Fungal infection of the nails.
A drop in blood pressure when standing up, causing dizziness or fainting.
Death of jaw bone tissue, so the bone is exposed in the mouth. Linked to bisphosphonates, especially after dental procedures.
Damage to the inner ear caused by a drug, leading to hearing loss, ringing in the ears or balance problems.
The feeling that the heart is pounding, racing or skipping beats.
Inflammation of the pancreas, causing severe upper abdominal pain that often spreads to the back.
A procedure that drains fluid from the abdomen with a needle.
Unusual behaviors during sleep, such as sleepwalking, sleep-driving or eating while not fully awake.
Tingling, prickling or numbness, often in the hands or feet.
Symptoms like those of Parkinson's disease, such as tremor, stiffness and slow movement. Drugs that block dopamine can cause it.
A serious gum infection that damages the tissue and bone that hold the teeth.
Damage to the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, causing numbness, tingling or pain, usually in the hands and feet.
Sore throat from inflammation of the pharynx.
Inflammation of a vein, often at an IV site, with pain, redness and swelling.
Increased sensitivity of the skin to sunlight, which leads to sunburn or rash more easily.
Excessive thirst.
Producing a large amount of urine.
High blood pressure during pregnancy with signs of organ damage, such as protein in the urine.
A painful erection that lasts for hours without sexual stimulation. It is a medical emergency.
Able to cause a new abnormal heart rhythm or make an existing one worse.
A rare, often fatal reaction to long or high-dose propofol infusions, with metabolic acidosis, muscle breakdown, heart failure and kidney failure.
Treatment given to prevent a disease or condition.
Itching.
Scarring of lung tissue, which makes the lungs stiff and breathing difficult.
A kidney infection, usually spread up from the bladder.
A longer time for the heart to recharge between beats, seen on an ECG. It raises the risk of torsades de pointes.
Slow, shallow breathing that lowers oxygen and raises carbon dioxide in the blood. It is the main cause of death in opioid overdose.
Damage to the retina caused by a drug, which can permanently harm vision.
Breakdown of muscle tissue that releases muscle proteins into the blood. These proteins can damage the kidneys.
Excess saliva or drooling.
Sleepiness or drowsiness.
Stiff, tight muscles caused by damage to the brain or spinal cord.
Infection of the fluid in the abdomen (ascites) without an obvious source, seen in patients with cirrhosis.
A seizure that does not stop, or repeated seizures without recovery in between. It is a medical emergency.
A rare, severe drug reaction in which the skin and the linings of the mouth, eyes and genitals blister and peel.
Inflammation and sores in the mouth.
Fainting: a brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain.
An abnormal heart rhythm with a fast rate.
A heart rate that is faster than normal.
Involuntary, repetitive movements, often of the face, lips and tongue, that develop after long-term use of dopamine-blocking drugs. It may be permanent.
Inflammation of a tendon.
A low platelet count, which raises the risk of bleeding and bruising.
Related to a blood clot that forms in a vessel and can break loose and block a vessel elsewhere, as in stroke, heart attack or pulmonary embolism.
A dangerous type of ventricular tachycardia linked to QT prolongation. It can turn into ventricular fibrillation.
A more severe form of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, with blistering and peeling over a large part of the skin.
A person whose genes make a drug-metabolizing enzyme (such as CYP2D6) work faster than usual. For codeine and tramadol, this produces more of the active opioid than expected.
A person whose genes make a drug-metabolizing enzyme work slowly or not at all. A prodrug that needs that enzyme to become active works less well.
Hives: raised, itchy welts on the skin.
Hot flashes and night sweats, as seen in menopause.
A blood clot in a vein: deep vein thrombosis (usually in the leg) or pulmonary embolism (in the lungs).
A chaotic rhythm in the lower chambers of the heart, so the heart quivers instead of pumping. It causes cardiac arrest.
A fast heart rhythm that starts in the lower chambers of the heart. It can cause fainting or cardiac arrest.
A feeling that you or the room is spinning.
Development of male traits, such as body hair, a deeper voice and acne, in females or children, from exposure to androgens such as testosterone.
Very dry skin.
Dry mouth.
The adrenal glands make too little cortisol. Stopping corticosteroids suddenly after long use can cause it.
A non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate that makes urination difficult.

An infection with Candida yeast. Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) affects the mouth and throat; vulvovaginal candidiasis is a vaginal yeast infection; invasive candidiasis is in the blood or organs.
A bacterium that can overgrow in the colon after antibiotics kill normal gut bacteria, causing diarrhea and colitis.
Removing bacteria (such as MRSA) that live on the body, often in the nose, without causing infection, to prevent later infection or spread.
A dangerous complication of diabetes in which a lack of insulin leads to high blood sugar and a buildup of ketones that make the blood acidic.
Sores in the lining of the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.
Damage to the lining of the esophagus from stomach acid, seen in severe reflux.
Stomach contents flow back into the esophagus, causing heartburn.
Fungal (yeast) infections of the genitals.
Breast cancer whose cells have receptors for estrogen or progesterone, so hormone therapy can slow its growth.
Affecting both the skin and the moist linings of the body, such as the mouth.
A sleep disorder with overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden attacks of sleep.
Related to a tumor or cancer.
A scale that grades heart failure by how much physical activity causes symptoms. Higher classes mean symptoms appear with less activity.
Sores in the lining of the stomach or duodenum.
High blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs, which strains the right side of the heart.
An uncomfortable feeling in the legs with an urge to move them, mostly in the evening or at night.
Acid-lowering drugs given to critically ill hospital patients to prevent stomach bleeding from stress ulcers.
Fungal skin infections, such as athlete's foot, jock itch and ringworm.
Drugs started soon after a possible exposure to an infection, such as HIV, to prevent it.
Drugs taken before possible exposure to an infection, such as HIV, to prevent it.
Treatment given after the main treatment, such as surgery, to lower the chance the cancer comes back.
A patient who has taken opioids regularly long enough that the body has adapted to them. High-potency opioid products are only for these patients.
The body has adapted to a drug, so stopping it suddenly causes withdrawal symptoms. It is not the same as addiction.
The same dose of a drug has less effect over time, so a higher dose is needed for the same effect.
Symptoms that occur when a drug the body has adapted to is stopped or reduced quickly.
Drugs that slow the CYP3A4 liver enzyme. Drugs broken down by that enzyme then build up to higher levels.
Drugs that speed up the CYP3A4 liver enzyme, which lowers levels of drugs it breaks down. Stopping an inducer makes those levels rise again.
A needle placed into the spinal canal, as in a lumbar puncture or spinal anesthesia.
The space just outside the covering of the spinal cord, where some anesthetics and pain drugs are injected.
New cancers caused by earlier cancer treatment.
An inherited condition in which tumors form in several hormone-producing glands, such as the thyroid, parathyroid and adrenal glands.
